heading|1|I|Which treats of the character and pursuits of the famous gentleman Don Quixote of La Mancha|1|1||3|14|lead=In a village of La Mancha, the name of which I have no desire to call to mind, there lived not long since one of those gentlemen that keep a lance in the lance-rack, an old buckler, a lean hack, and a greyhound for coursing.||:Which treats of the character and pursuits of the famous gentleman Don Quixote of La Mancha|||||
heading|1|II|Which treats of the first sally the ingenious Don Quixote made from home|1|1||11|22|lead=These preliminaries settled, he did not care to put off any longer the execution of his design, urged on to it by the thought of all the world was losing by his delay, seeing what wrongs he intended to right, grievances to redress, injustices to repair, abuses to remove, and duties to discharge.||:Which treats of the first sally the ingenious Don Quixote made from home|||||
heading|1|III|Wherein is related the droll way in which Don Quixote had himself dubbed a knight|1|1||19|30|lead=Harassed by this reflection, he made haste with his scanty pothouse supper, and having finished it called the landlord, and shutting himself into the stable with him, fell on his knees before him, saying, “From this spot I rise not, valiant knight, until your courtesy grants me the boon I seek, one that will redound to your praise and the benefit of the human race.”||:Wherein is related the droll way in which Don Quixote had himself dubbed a knight|||||
heading|1|IV|Of what happened to our knight when he left the inn|1|1||29|40|lead=Day was dawning when Don Quixote quitted the inn, so happy, so gay, so exhilarated at finding himself now dubbed a knight, that his joy was like to burst his horse-girths.||:Of what happened to our knight when he left the inn|||||
heading|1|V|In which the narrative of our knight’s mishap is continued|1|1||39|50|lead=Finding, then, that, in fact he could not move, he thought himself of having recourse to his usual remedy, which was to think of some passage in his books, and his craze brought to his mind that about Baldwin and the Marquis of Mantua, when Carloto left him wounded on the mountainside, a story known by heart by the children, not forgotten by the young men, and lauded and even believed by the old folk; and for all that not a whit truer than the miracles of Mahomet.||:In which the narrative of our knight’s mishap is continued|||||
heading|1|VI|Of the diverting and important scrutiny which the curate and the barber made in the library of our ingenious gentleman|1|1||47|58|lead=He was still sleeping; so the curate asked the niece for the keys of the room where the books, the authors of all the mischief, were, and right willingly she gave them.||:Of the diverting and important scrutiny which the curate and the barber made in the library of our ingenious gentleman|||||
heading|1|VII|Of the second sally of our worthy knight Don Quixote of La Mancha|1|1||55|66|lead=At this instant Don Quixote began shouting out, “Here, here, valiant knights! here is need for you to put forth the might of your strong arms, for they of the Court are gaining the mastery in the tourney!”||:Of the second sally of our worthy knight Don Quixote of La Mancha|||||
heading|1|VIII|Of the good fortune which the valiant Don Quixote had in the terrible and undreamt-of adventure of the windmills, with other occurrences worthy to be fitly recorded|1|1||63|74|lead=At this point they came in sight of thirty or forty windmills that there are on that plain, and as soon as Don Quixote saw them he said to his squire, “Fortune is arranging matters for us better than we could have shaped our desires ourselves, for look there, friend Sancho Panza, where thirty or more monstrous giants present themselves, all of whom I mean to engage in battle and slay, and with whose spoils we shall begin to make our fortunes; for this is righteous warfare, and it is God’s good service to sweep so evil a breed from off the face of the earth.”||:Of the good fortune which the valiant Don Quixote had in the terrible and undreamt-of adventure of the windmills, with other occurrences worthy to be fitly recorded|||||

heading|1|IX|In which is concluded and finished the terrific battle between the gallant Biscayan and the valiant Manchegan|1|1||77|88|lead=In the First Part of this history we left the valiant Biscayan and the renowned Don Quixote with drawn swords uplifted, ready to deliver two such furious slashing blows that if they had fallen full and fair they would at least have split and cleft them asunder from top to toe and laid them open like a pomegranate; and at this so critical point the delightful history came to a stop and stood cut short without any intimation from the author where what was missing was to be found.||:In which is concluded and finished the terrific battle between the gallant Biscayan and the valiant Manchegan|||||
heading|1|X|Of the pleasant discourse that passed between Don Quixote and his squire Sancho Panza|1|1||83|94|lead=Now by this time Sancho had risen, rather the worse for the handling of the friars’ muleteers, and stood watching the battle of his master, Don Quixote, and praying to God in his heart that it might be his will to grant him the victory, and that he might thereby win some island to make him governor of, as he had promised.||:Of the pleasant discourse that passed between Don Quixote and his squire Sancho Panza|||||
heading|1|XI|What befell Don Quixote with certain goatherds|1|1||91|102|lead=He was cordially welcomed by the goatherds, and Sancho, having as best he could put up Rocinante and the ass, drew towards the fragrance that came from some pieces of salted goat simmering in a pot on the fire; and though he would have liked at once to try if they were ready to be transferred from the pot to the stomach, he refrained from doing so as the goatherds removed them from the fire, and laying sheepskins on the ground, quickly spread their rude table, and with signs of hearty good-will invited them both to share what they had.||:What befell Don Quixote with certain goatherds|||||
heading|1|XII|Of what a goatherd related to those with Don Quixote|1|1||101|112|lead=Just then another young man, one of those who fetched their provisions from the village, came up and said, “Do you know what is going on in the village, comrades?”||:Of what a goatherd related to those with Don Quixote|||||
heading|1|XIII|In which is ended the story of the shepherdess Marcela, with other incidents|1|1||109|120|lead=But hardly had day begun to show itself through the balconies of the east, when five of the six goatherds came to rouse Don Quixote and tell him that if he was still of a mind to go and see the famous burial of Chrysostom they would bear him company.||:In which is ended the story of the shepherdess Marcela, with other incidents|||||

This edition gathers the preface and the first fourteen chapters of the 1605 book, with the plates Gustave Doré drew in 1863.;quote=In a village of La Mancha, the name of which I have no desire to call to mind, there lived not long since one of those gentlemen that keep a lance in the lance-rack, an old buckler, a lean hack, and a greyhound for coursing.;style=contraportada;toc=false||:Back cover|||||
